what: Enel Chile generates and distributes electricity in Chile. It owns hydroelectric, wind, solar and thermal power plants, and runs the distribution network that delivers electricity to homes and businesses in and around Santiago, serving a large share of the country’s population.
customers: Chilean households and businesses receiving electricity through its regulated distribution network, plus industrial customers and other utilities buying power under contract.
money: Electricity from hydroelectric, wind, solar and thermal plants sold under contract and into the market.
Regulated delivery of electricity to end customers in the Santiago region.
moat: Electricity distribution in a defined area is a legal monopoly with tariffs set by the regulator, which makes the revenue predictable and the position unassailable. On the generation side, Chile has exceptional solar and wind resources and Enel Chile’s hydroelectric plants are long-lived assets that cannot be replicated — the good sites are taken.
risks: Revenue has swung widely, from $2.8B in 2021 to $4.9B in 2022 and back to $4.0B in 2024, because electricity costs and tariff mechanisms move together.
Chilean regulated tariffs are set by the government, and tariff decisions during periods of high energy costs have squeezed distributors before.
Hydroelectric output depends on rainfall, and Chile has experienced extended drought which forced expensive thermal generation and market purchases.
The shares trade in dollars while the earnings are in Chilean pesos, so currency movements alone change the return.
Five analysts average a $4.77 target, about 19% above the current price.
opportunities: The shares trade at about 9.6 times earnings, 7.1 times EV/EBITDA and 6.8 times free cash flow.
Free cash flow of $815.6M against a $5.5B market value is a 15% yield.
Regulated distribution in the Santiago region is a monopoly position with predictable, inflation-linked revenue.
Chile has among the best solar resources in the world, and the renewable build-out lowers the cost of generation over time.
No debt reported at the parent level, with $380.7M of cash.
watch: Hydroelectric generation volumes and the regulated tariff decisions. Rainfall determines the cost of serving customers and the regulator determines what can be charged, and those two together are the business.
view: Utilities in emerging markets are usually cheap for one of two reasons: the regulator is unpredictable or the currency is. In Chile’s case, the regulator is actually among the more credible in Latin America, and the currency is the main source of the discount. At 9.6 times earnings, 7.1 times EV/EBITDA and a 15% free cash flow yield, Enel Chile is priced as though Chile were a riskier place than it is.

The business has two halves with quite different characters. Distribution in the Santiago region is a legal monopoly with tariffs set by the regulator — predictable, inflation-linked, and about as safe as revenue gets. Generation is the variable half, and the variable within it is rainfall. Chile’s hydroelectric plants are excellent long-lived assets on sites that cannot be replicated, but when drought reduces their output, the company must buy power or burn gas to meet its contracts, which is expensive. Chile’s extended drought has been the single largest determinant of this company’s results.

The renewable build-out is the structural improvement and it is substantial. Chile has among the best solar resources in the world and strong wind in the south, and as that capacity comes online the cost of generating electricity falls and the dependence on rainfall and imported fuel diminishes. That is a genuine long-term change in the economics rather than a cyclical one.

What a dollar investor has to accept is that the earnings are in pesos, the dividend is in pesos, and a currency move can erase an operating year’s progress without anything happening to the business. That is the actual risk here, more than regulation or rainfall, and it is not hedgeable within the position. My view is that this is a reasonably priced monopoly distributor plus an improving generation portfolio, offered at a discount for country risk that is real but smaller than the market applies. Watch hydro volumes and tariff decisions; they explain almost every surprise this company produces.
bull: Solar and wind build-out cuts generation costs and drought dependence while a monopoly distribution network delivers inflation-linked revenue at a 15% free cash flow yield.
bear: Extended drought forces expensive thermal purchases, tariff decisions squeeze the distributor, and peso weakness erases the dollar investor’s return.
